title: How a consumer brand should write an about page
metaTitle: How a brand should write its about page
excerpt: Name who makes the object and why that matters to a shopper who does not know you. Skip the origin myth unless it changes the decision to see the product.

faqs.question: Who should a product about page name?
faqs.answer: Name the person accountable for the goods: the maker, the pattern cutter, the person who handles a fault. Say the job and the fact that changes quality. A workshop portrait with the object in the frame beats a rented-wall headshot.

faqs.question: When should a brand admit a factory?
faqs.answer: When a shopper could mistake the goods for bench-made. A plain sentence about a workshop you have worked with, and patterns you own, is an honorable method. Concealing it collapses at the first detailed question.

faqs.question: What should the page leave out?
faqs.answer: Leave trophy language and invented quotes off the lead. Press logos can sit low, small, and only if they are real. End on the product, so the reader returns to the object with a clearer reason.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A consumer brand about page is proof that people stand behind the object. Name who makes the work, or who is responsible for it, and why a shopper who does not know you should care. Skip the origin myth unless that story changes the decision to see the product.

The page answers a practical suspicion. Is there a person I could picture if the order goes wrong, and is the way they make this thing relevant to the thing I just looked at. A founding legend rarely answers that.

## Name who does the work

Start with the people a shopper is trusting. The maker, the designer, the person who answers email about a fault. A photograph in the workshop or the studio, with the object in the frame, beats a portrait against a rented wall. Under the name, write the job in one line and the fact that changes quality. Throws the mugs. Cuts the patterns. Checks every hem. Replies to repairs.

"Obsessed with detail" fits every about page in your category. "Glazes each mug and discards the ones that warp" is a fact a shopper can use. Specifics are the proof. If a small team shares the work, say the team and the roles. Pretending a collective is a lone artisan, or the reverse, will snag on the first workshop visit or the first honest interview.

Google's guide to [people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) treats "who" as part of trust. On a product brand, the who is the person accountable for the goods, not a hidden byline on the essay. Make them visible. Trust matters more, in that guidance, than a stack of atmosphere. A shopper who can name the role will forgive a plain page. A shopper who cannot find a human will wonder who receives the money.

Keep the names current. A maker who has left should not still be "at the bench" in September. Stale people are a falsehood the customer may notice in a reply signed by someone else. Review the page when the team changes, on the same calendar as you review materials.

## Why this shopper should care

Connect the person to the object. The shopper cares that a named potter accepts the variation in the glaze, because they saw the variation on the product page. They care that repairs go back to the same bench. They care that sizing is graded by someone who publishes the measurements. They do not care, yet, that you met your co-founder in a city they have not visited.

Write one short block for the doubt your product actually raises. Handmade variation. A stiff denim that softens. A price that is higher because the sole can be replaced. Answer that doubt with the person and the method. Then offer the way to see the product, in the same words as the homepage. An about page that ends on a poem forgets the errand. The errand was to decide whether the object has someone behind it.

Behavior beats a values list. We publish the measurements. We answer fault emails within a few days, if you keep that promise. We show the glaze including the ones with iron spots. Anyone can typeset integrity, craft, and community. Fewer brands can describe what happens when a cup arrives chipped.

If you work with a factory, say so when the shopper could mistake the goods for bench-made. "Cut and sewn with a workshop we have worked with for six years, to patterns we own" is an honorable sentence. Concealing the method is not craft. It is a story that collapses at the first detailed question. The about page is where the method can be calm and exact.

## When an origin story earns its place

An origin story earns space when it changes the product in front of the shopper. You started making the refill because the bottle was being thrown away, and the refill is the thing you sell now. You moved the weave to a heavier cloth after the first batch pilled, and the current cloth is the heavy one. Those sentences help someone choose.

A story about a trip, a grandparent, or a manifesto of slow living can be a sentence, or a journal essay for people who already bought. It should not lead. Leading with it asks a stranger to adopt your biography before you have shown them a durable reason. Some biographies are lovely. They are still second.

If the age of the company matters, make it one line attached to a present-tense fact. "We have repaired this shoe since 2014, and we still do." The repair is the point. The year is the support. A timeline with twenty dates will be skipped. Nielsen Norman Group's piece on [how long people stay](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) says visitors often leave within 10 to 20 seconds and read only about a quarter of the text. Spend the quarter on the person and the method.

If you tell a longer story, use scenes a customer can check. The bench. The material. The decision to drop a style that looked good and failed in use. Avoid a cinematic voice. The reader can buy the object this week. Write as if they might.

## Method, materials, and the limit of the claim

Materials belong on this page only when they are more than a list of virtues. Where the clay comes from, if you know. Why this leather. What you do not use, stated without a sneer at other brands. A claim you cannot explain should come off the page. "Sustainable" with no method is a manifesto wearing a lab coat. "Replaceable sole, spare buttons in the hem" is a method.

Show the limit. Small batches mean a color can sell out. Handmade means two mugs from the same glaze will not match. Say that next to the romance, or the romance will be read as a warranty you did not intend. The product page should agree. If the about page celebrates variation and the product page promises uniformity, fix one of them before you publish.

Wabisabi, a public Hanabi brand site, is a useful reference for tone: calm, tactile, unwilling to shout. Borrow the calm. Do not borrow a story that is not yours. Down the Cove shows the other half of brand truth, a shop whose goods survived a migration and a redesign. The about page of a shop should still be true after the redesign. Pretty type does not license a new biography.

Photographs should include hands or tools and the object. A landscape with no product is a travel ad. A face with no product is a portrait studio. The argument of this page is that these people make that thing. Put both in the frame when you can.

## What to leave off

Leave the trophy language off the lead. Press logos, award badges, and "as seen in" can sit low, small, and only if they are real. They are not the proof that the mug is well made. A shopper who does not know you yet cannot use a badge as a substitute for the object.

Leave off invented quotes. A testimonial needs a real customer, a real permission, and a specific sentence. "Changed my mornings" is filler. "The 300 ml cup fits the shelf I already had" is evidence. Hanabi does not invent client quotes, and a product brand should not invent customer quotes to fill a layout.

Leave the page shorter than the workshop diary in your head. Two people, one method, one limit, one path to the product. That page can be read on a phone while the other tab holds the mug. A history essay cannot. Facilities and studios deserve one concrete line if a visit is possible. If visits are not possible, do not imply an open door you will have to refuse.

## Make the heading match the proof

Title the page for what it contains. "The workshop" or "Who makes this" is clearer than "Our story" when the content is people and method. Google's title guidance wants the title and the main heading to describe the page, and it will lean on the visible heading when the title is vague. Promote the heading that matches the proof.

Use the brand name once. Repeating it in every subheading sounds like a template. Write in the same voice as the product page. Short sentences. The object named in the same words. If the product page says Coast mug and the about page says "our vessel," the shopper has to translate. Translation is a tax. You are the one who should pay it, by picking one name.

End on the product. See it. The about page is a success when the reader returns to the object with a clearer reason, not when they have finished your biography.

## One decision, told as proof

Some shoppers want a single story of a choice: why you changed the cloth, why you offer repair, why a collaboration ended. A proof page can hold that constraint and that decision, then return them to the product. That is [proof pages for a consumer brand](/blog/proof-pages-for-a-consumer-brand).

If you want to talk through who belongs on the page, and which sentence changes a purchase, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the names of the people who make the work, and the object they should be standing next to.
